summary: Defines a standards-track MIB for the management of applications, giving SNMP tools standard objects to monitor software running on systems.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard way to ask a computer which programs are running and how they are doing.

questions: what is the application management mib
how does the application mib relate to the system application mib
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a manager see and control what applications are doing inside, with the application's help.

tldr.problem: The earlier System Application MIB could only report what is visible without the cooperation of the software, so it said little about throughput, response time, open files or connections, or how to control an application.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB adds tables for service-level views, open and former I/O channels with transaction statistics, and per-process status and control, all tied to the System Application MIB through the running application element index.
tldr.outcome: It gives SNMP managers a generic base for monitoring and controlling almost any application, provided the application is instrumented to report the data. It is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no replacement.

today: RFC 2564 is a Proposed Standard from May 1999, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Application MIB Adds
sections.content:
RFC 2564 defines the Application Management MIB, a set of SNMP-readable objects for managing applications. It complements the System Application MIB, which covers the common attributes of applications that can be observed without the software's cooperation.

Because the earlier MIB did not require application instrumentation, many topics were left out. This document brings several of them into scope: generic throughput measurement, letting a managed entity report what it counts as a unit of work, response time monitoring, applications distributed within one managed system, resource use such as files in use and I/O statistics, and control actions such as stopping, suspending, resuming or asking for reconfiguration (for example a SIGHUP).

The authors say it builds on experience from the Host Resources MIB, the Network Services Monitoring MIB, the Mail Monitoring MIB, the RDBMS MIB, the Entity MIB and work on World Wide Web servers, and abstracts out what those have in common.
sections.plainLanguage: An older list of questions could only ask things you can see from the outside. This one lets the program itself answer more detailed questions, like what files it has open.

sections.title: Tables, Shared Indexes and Related MIBs
sections.content:
The SNMP information model has no subclassing or multiple inheritance, so the MIB emulates them with tables that share common indexes. A single logical resource can therefore show up in several tables, possibly defined in different MIBs, and a management application has to recognize that. One table can also hold rows for many applications on the same system.

The key link to the System Application MIB is sysApplRunElmtIndex. Implementations of both MIBs on one platform must use a consistent policy for assigning this value to running application elements. The Host Resources MIB index hrSWRunIndex must likewise be consistent with it.

The Network Services Monitoring MIB is the base set of attributes for network applications, but because of differences in index representation, its relationship to this MIB is not formally defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Every running program gets a number, and all the lists use the same number for it. That way you can look the same program up in different lists.

sections.title: Services and the I/O Channel Group
sections.content:
The service-level tables identify named instances of services on a system and tie running application elements to them. There are four: service name to service instance, service instance to service name, service instance to running application element, and running application element to service instance. A service is not the same thing as a protocol. The text suggests SMTP and HTTP providers are good candidates for services and finger probably is not, and implementors may define more.

The I/O channel group models data an application handles as channels, such as files and network connections. Each entry in the open channels table (open time, read and write requests, bytes, last read and write times) has a matching entry in either the open files table (file name, size, read or write mode) or the open connections table (transport protocol, near-end and far-end address and port, application protocol).

The first index of these tables says whether the second index is a running application element or a service instance, and the third identifies the channel within that context.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a list of the jobs a computer does, and a list of every file and network chat each program has open right now.

sections.title: Transaction Statistics
sections.content:
Channel traffic can be structured as transactions. The simple model is an invoker sending a request to a performer, which returns a response. Because some protocols let one entity play both roles, counts are kept for transmitted and received requests and responses, in both transactions and bytes.

Three tables carry the detail. The transaction stream summary table holds per-stream totals, including a human-readable description of what the stream counts as a unit of work and cumulative times spent waiting for responses, receiving them, handling requests and sending responses. The transaction flow statistics table splits counts by direction and by request or response. The transaction kind statistics table breaks them down further by transaction kind.
sections.plainLanguage: It counts how many questions a program asked and answered, how big they were, and how long it spent waiting.

sections.title: History, Status and Control
sections.content:
The former channel group keeps history about channels that have closed. A control table decides, for each running application element or service instance, whether history is kept, how many records and for how long, and counts entries deleted early to make room. Former connection, former file and transaction history tables parallel the open-channel tables.

The running element status table reports current heap usage, the current number of open network connections and the most recent error status message. The control table lets a manager with the right permissions suspend and resume an element, request reconfiguration or request termination.
sections.plainLanguage: It remembers what a program used to have open, tells you how much memory it is using, and lets a grown-up pause or stop it.

sections.title: Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Unlike the System Application MIB, much of this MIB needs instrumentation built into the managed resource. Some tables might be served by one monitor process, while others are spread across the managed system. That means the system's management infrastructure must let different subagents own different rows of one table. The text names AgentX as one subagent protocol that supports this.

Some objects may be costly at run time. Timing each transaction could need two kernel calls per transaction, and keeping per-transaction tables instead of aggregates could hurt storage and performance. Also, unless service instance indexes are allocated without collisions, the service-level tables need an index-reservation mechanism.

The MIB uses 64-bit counters where values may grow fast, along with 32-bit counters holding the low-order 32 bits, so SNMPv1, SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 environments can all use it. Rows come and go with the application elements, so each has its own discontinuity indicators rather than relying on sysUpTime.0.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping all these numbers can slow a program down, so the people building it have to be careful about how much they count.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Making this information reachable from outside can become a security problem. The tables separate sensitive control from less sensitive usage information. Suspend and resume, reconfigure and terminate are in separate columns, so access control can allow "reconfigure" but not "kill".

The MIB is useful to managers with read-only access, though in some environments even read-only access may need to be restricted. The text adds that the MIB can help a security administrator monitor how much an application is used and check the integrity of application components.
sections.plainLanguage: The buttons that stop a program are kept apart from the ones that just look, so you can give someone a peek without handing over the off switch.
